title: Indian EB-2 Queue Stays Frozen in 2013 as Premium Processing Rule Reaches White House
headline: Indian EB-2 Queue Stays Frozen in 2013 as Premium Processing Rule Reaches White House
subheadline: The November 2026 Visa Bulletin held India's EB-2 final action date at November 1, 2013 for a second month, while a USCIS proposal to amend premium processing timeframes entered OIRA review on October 13 with its text still secret.
body:
• The November 2026 Visa Bulletin keeps India's EB-2 final action date at November 1, 2013 — unchanged for a second straight month — while most other countries advanced three months to April 1, 2025.
  • A USCIS proposed rule titled "Amending the Premium Processing Timeframe" (RIN 1615-AD25) entered White House OIRA review on October 13; its text is not public, so no one yet knows whether premium deadlines would lengthen or shorten.
  • Reader check: if you are an Indian EB-2 applicant in the US with a priority date before January 15, 2015, the November Dates for Filing chart is the filing benchmark — but a green card can only be approved if your priority date is before November 1, 2013. Confirm the chart USCIS designates for November on its filing-chart page before filing.
  • India's EB-3 final action date did move, by three weeks to January 22, 2014; EB-1 India stayed at February 1, 2023.

Indian professionals in the EB-2 advanced-degree green card queue saw no movement for a second straight month. The US State Department's Visa Bulletin for November 2026 keeps the EB-2 final action date for India at November 1, 2013, IANS reported, while the date for most other countries advanced three months, from January 1, 2025 to April 1, 2025. China-born EB-2 applicants stayed at October 1, 2021. The Murthy Law Firm's summary of the bulletin confirms the same dates.

At the same time, a second process that matters to the same workers moved quietly in Washington. A Department of Homeland Security proposal to change the deadlines for paid premium processing — the expedited service H-1B employers rely on — is under review at the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA). According to the reginfo.gov listing cited by IANS, OIRA received the USCIS proposed rule, "Amending the Premium Processing Timeframe" (RIN 1615-AD25), on October 13. It is listed as pending review, with no legal deadline, and is not designated economically significant.

Two clocks, neither moving for India

The final action date is the cutoff that decides whether a green card can actually be issued: only applicants whose priority date falls before it can be approved. For Indian EB-2 applicants, that line has effectively been stuck near the end of 2013 because demand from India far exceeds the per-country limit, which the November bulletin restates as 7% of the combined family and employment-based limits, or 25,620 visas. India's EB-2 category was unavailable in the last months of fiscal 2026 before reopening at the November 1, 2013 date in October.

There was modest movement elsewhere in India's employment-based rows. The EB-3 final action date advanced three weeks to January 22, 2014, with EB-3 Other Workers moving to the same date, while most other countries reached June 15, 2024 in EB-3. EB-1 India held at February 1, 2023, and the EB-5 unreserved date for Indian investors held at December 1, 2023.

"Imagine waiting 179 years for a green card. That's the projected wait for Indian green card applicants."

— Rep. Josh Gottheimer, on X

The quote, from New Jersey Democrat Josh Gottheimer, reflects an August analysis by the National Foundation for American Policy projecting a potential 179-year wait for an Indian national filing in EB-2 in January 2026 or later. Gottheimer has renewed his call to end per-country caps on employment-based green cards. NFAP estimated Indians make up about 79% — roughly 996,599 people — of the 1,264,495 waiting in the first three employment-based preferences as of December 2025.

What the premium processing review could change

Premium processing is the paid service under which USCIS guarantees action on eligible petitions within a set window — currently 15 business days for most I-129 and I-140 petitions. The proposal's text has not been made public, and the OIRA listing does not say which visa categories would be affected or whether deadlines would be lengthened or shortened. Until a proposed rule is published in the Federal Register and finalised, current timeframes govern and nothing changes for pending cases. A separate USCIS proposed rule, "Reforming the H-1B Nonimmigrant Visa Classification Program" (RIN 1615-AD00), has been pending at OIRA since August 24 and is designated economically significant.

What to do now

For November, IANS reported that USCIS says adjustment-of-status applicants in employment-based categories must use the Dates for Filing chart, under which Indian EB-2 and EB-3 applicants with priority dates before January 15, 2015 can file adjustment applications — filing is not approval, which still requires a priority date before the final action cutoff. Check the USCIS adjustment-of-status filing charts page before relying on the filing chart for a November filing. Employers using premium processing should watch the Federal Register: the first public sight of the new timeframe proposal will be its published text, not the OIRA listing.
